newsitem.title: UK: BOE renews argument for access to euro-credit.
newsitem.headline: BOE renews argument for access to euro-credit.

text.p: The Bank of England said on Thursday use of the planned payments system for the single currency would be more costly if countries outside of European Monetary Union did not get full access to intraday credit.

BOE deputy director Jown Townend said it was generally agreed that all European Union countries could link their payments systems to TARGET -- the acronym for Trans-European Automated Real-time Gross-Settlement Express Transfer.

But some argue that intraday liquidity should be denied to, or at least restricted in, the non-euro member countries, "apparently on the grounds that it could otherwise complicate the implementation of the single monetary policy."
Townend said others, including the Bank of England, believe that access to intraday liquidity was a natural corollary of extending national settlement systems across borders.

"They...see no grounds for any discrimination and argue that the potential spillover into overnight credit can be deterred quite adequately through penal interest, as it is in our own present Real Time Gross Settlement System," Townend said.

"The only effect of denying or restricting intraday liquidity in this case would be to increase somewhat the cost of using TARGET and so to encourage the use of alternative, rather less secure, payments arrangements, such as correspondent banking arrangements or the private sector ECU net settlement system (which will become euro)."

Townend said any such restriction would be unlikely to deter the international use of the euro significantly -- if that were the objective -- any more than lack of direct access to national settlement systems deters international use of existing currencies.
He said the Bank hoped to be able to resolve the issue "through the ongoing technical dialogue" in the European Monetary Institute, the fore-runner of the European Central Bank (ECB).
European monetary sources say negotiations over access to euro payments credit are at a stalemate, and the issue is unlikely to be settled before the ECB is formed in 1998.

This means that only countries launching the euro in January 1999 will be able to decide the issue. EU members unlikely to take part in EMU fear their banks will not be able to get needed euro funds as quickly or as cheaply as their EMU counterparts.

The Bundesbank is among the more vociferous opponents of granting access to non-euro member countries, arguing that to do so could disrupt the ECB's attempts to control monetary policy because it would boost liquidity and money supply outside its area of direct control.
